title: Prediction Is Not Reality
learningGoals: Compare a forecast with an observation

deeperExplanation.question: What if I have been right about this word before?
deeperExplanation.answer: Past experience is information, but the exact conditions of a new moment can differ. You can acknowledge that the word has taken effort without deciding every future detail. Notice what response the prediction invites: hiding, rehearsing or asking for time. Then choose what would serve the actual purpose. You do not have to promise yourself an easy word in order to attempt a useful message.

sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Prediction Is Not Reality. You see a name you may need to say. Your mind predicts a block, the listener’s impatience and the embarrassment afterwards. The conversation has not happened, but your body is already responding.

In this session, we will separate known facts from predictions, leave uncertainty open, and compare a forecast with an observation. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: A prediction is an attempt to forecast an event. It may feel vivid and familiar without being the event itself. We will distinguish what you know now from what you expect. You may know that a word has been difficult before. You do not yet know exactly how this moment will unfold, what the listener will think or how you will respond.

sections.narration:
You see a name you may need to say. Your mind predicts a block, the listener’s impatience and the embarrassment afterwards. The conversation has not happened, but your body is already responding.

The goal is not to replace a negative prediction with a positive guarantee. Both demand certainty about the future. A more useful response can be: this is uncertain, and I can choose my next small action. That action might be to say the name, ask for time or choose a setting you are willing to practise in.

Record only when you choose. Afterwards save one observation rather than decide what this says about you as a person.

sections.narration: For this next attempt, keep one clear purpose. Try another short request and describe what actually happened. Changed, unchanged or uncertain experiences are all information.

sections.narration: A prediction can sometimes be accurate. This does not make it a rule for every occasion. The exercise is about relating to forecasts more flexibly, not proving your mind wrong. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Before a manageable speaking moment, write one prediction and later one observation. Keep the observation specific. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
